A Ukrainian kamikaze drone crashed into one of the bridge’s arches at 5.38am local time, local channels reported. Earlier drones could be heard buzzing above the structure, as Russian air defence units opened fire.
The extent of the damage was unclear. One report said the arch was listing at a 15-degree angle and “looked tired”.
The Kremlin-appointed governor of Crimea, Sergey Aksyonov, confirmed the “enemy” had launched an attack. “As a result, traffic will be restricted, likely until the afternoon,” he wrote on Telegram.
Related: Ukraine war briefing: Energy attacks made possible by continuing Starshield restrictions, says Zelenskyy
Russian officials said the crossing would remain closed while experts assessed its condition. About 2,000 vehicles were reportedly stuck in traffic jams on both sides.
In a call with reporters, the Kremlin spokesperson, Dmitry Peskov, downplayed the incident. He said: “Minor damage is being assessed. ⁠Traffic across the bridge continues.”
Ukraine says the bridge is a legitimate target for its armed forces, and has made at least two previous attempts to blow it up.

In 2022 a truck laden with explosives damaged part of the road section. A second strike using a “sea baby” drone took place the following year. Russia has subsequently strengthened air defences and installed metal barges and boom barriers.

Overnight Ukraine launched 1,336 drones, in what the Kremlin says was one of the biggest attacks so far this year. About 600 were intercepted at night on their approach to Moscow, claimed the capital’s mayor, Sergei Sobyanin, and more than 150 more throughout Monday.

The barrage took place days before a summit in Shenzhen between China’s president, Xi Jinping, Donald Trump and Putin. US officials say the talks will not focus on the war in Ukraine, where Russia’s military offensive has largely stalled.

Ukraine says its retaliatory strikes are justified retribution for Russia’s own missile and drone barrages of its cities and energy grid – attacks that have killed hundreds of civilians and regularly knock out power and heating for millions. In recent weeks Russia has repeatedly hit two critical bridges in Kyiv over the Dnipro river.

Diplomatic efforts on ending the almost five-year war have so far gone nowhere. After a fresh round of talks in Abu Dhabi last week, Putin reiterated his hardline territorial demands and said any deployment of foreign troops would be seen in Moscow as a “continuation of war”.

The Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, said on Friday the Trump administration had proposed that Kyiv gives Russia the eastern Donbas region – including towns and villages Russia does not control – in exchange for Nato membership or Nato-like guarantees.

Zelenskyy ruled out handing over territory. The details of possible US security guarantees were vague and did not feature American troops on the ground, he said, citing conversations with Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner and the real-estate developer Steve Witkoff. The emissaries last week saw Putin in Moscow.

articles.title: Revealed: Israel uploaded millions of photos to Amazon’s facial recognition platform to track Palestinians
articles.summary: Upload came as the Israeli military was increasing its reliance on Amazon’s cloud platform to meet the technological demands of its bombardment of Gaza
body: The Israeli military uploaded 3.5m photos to Amazon’s cloud platform in order to use the US company’s facial recognition technology to analyse images of Palestinians, the Guardian can reveal.
Leaked documents show the expansive catalogue of images was moved into Amazon’s cloud in the early months of Israel’s devastating aerial bombardment and ground offensive in Gaza.
The images were uploaded by a department of the Israeli military that holds a vast collection of photos covering the Palestinian populations in Gaza and the West Bank.
The department informed Amazon of the decision to upload the images in early 2024 so it could use Rekognition, the company’s AI-powered image analysis platform for a facial recognition project.

The documents obtained by the Guardian form part of an investigation into the Israeli military’s reliance on the technology and infrastructure of Amazon’s cloud computing business to monitor Palestinians.

According to the files and interviews with military sources, Israel has in recent years migrated huge volumes of data – including sensitive intelligence material and information about Palestinians living under occupation – into Amazon’s datacentres.
The large set of images was moved into an Amazon datacentre near Tel Aviv by a department commonly known as Rolling Stone, which sits within a military software unit.
The department takes its name from a system widely used by the Israeli military that serves as a central repository of information about Palestinians living in Gaza and the West Bank.

At the time, the department was exploring using facial recognition technologies to analyse the extensive catalogues of images of Palestinians it holds, several sources with knowledge of its work said.

After Israel’s ground invasion of Gaza in October 2023, its military routinely collected images of Palestinians as they passed through checkpoints, often after they had been forcibly displaced by the bombing campaign.
It’s not clear whether the 3.5m images uploaded to Amazon’s Rekognition were captured at these checkpoints, which effectively served as pop-up surveillance posts.
However, a military source familiar with facial recognition efforts at the checkpoints said Amazon’s cloud infrastructure was used due to the “very large scale” of images collected at the sites.

Israel has long used facial recognition technology, particularly in its occupation of the West Bank. Face scanning is routine at checkpoints, while Israeli soldiers use custom-built smartphone apps to collect images of people living in the Palestinian territory.

In the early stages of its campaign in Gaza, Israel used Rekognition to identify hostages captured by militants in the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023. The military also deployed facial recognition technology to identify people it suspected were militants.

The New York Times has previously reported how the military experimented with commercially available technology in Gaza to detect faces in crowds and in drone footage, at times wrongly flagging civilians as militants.

The new documents reveal the Israeli military’s use of Amazon technology, both for experiments with facial recognition and for a more far-reaching project to move its data on to the servers of the computing arm of the conglomerate founded by billionaire Jeff Bezos.

They also shed light on what the Israeli military is moving into the cloud and how it uses Amazon Web Services (AWS) infrastructure to support the collection and processing of Palestinians’ personal data, typically gathered indiscriminately, through intrusive means and without their consent.

The files suggest the ties between AWS and the Israeli military deepened during a period in which Israel has been accused of committing grave crimes in Gaza, including genocide – a charge denied by Israel, but supported by a UN commission of inquiry, Israeli human rights groups and genocide experts.

A spokesperson for AWS said it had no “visibility” into workloads held by its customers in its cloud. They added: “We respect the privacy of our customers, and we do not discuss our relationship without their consent.”
In early 2024, a small group of Israeli soldiers worked from AWS’s offices in Tel Aviv, located on the 28th floor of one of Israel’s tallest skyscrapers.
The soldiers were exploring ways to use the company’s cloud infrastructure to more effectively operate a facial recognition programme underway in Gaza, several military sources said.

It’s not clear whether their work was made operational or if it related to the 3.5m images uploaded to Rekognition. The presence of the group at AWS’s offices, however, underscores the close relationship between the Israeli military and the cloud provider.

An AWS spokesperson said its customers “regularly visit our offices for briefings and meetings”. They added: “Any suggestion that these visits are anything other than routine customer engagement is wrong and unsubstantiated.”

The foundation of Israel’s relationship with Amazon is a sweeping 2021 contract known as Project Nimbus. Under the multibillion dollar deal, AWS and Google provide cloud services to a wide range of government and military clients.

The Guardian revealed last year that the Nimbus contract contains unusual terms that prohibit the US companies from restricting or suspending Israeli government and military use of their cloud services, even if Israel breaches their terms of service.

This would prevent the kind of unilateral action taken by Microsoft last year when it disabled the Israeli military’s access to technology used to operate a mass surveillance system uncovered by the Guardian and +972 Magazine.

As part of the Nimbus deal, AWS opened new datacentres in Israel in early 2023, allowing the Israeli government and military clients to migrate data from their own servers, according to documents. A large proportion of data was also moved from AWS datacentres in Ireland.

A central component of the Nimbus contract, files show, was an obligation on AWS to provide the Israeli military with access to a segregated area within its Tel Aviv datacentres, fortified with enhanced digital and physical security measures.

This isolated area within the AWS cloud – used to store sensitive material relating to military operations and intelligence collection – was described by the company and its client as a “walled garden”.

The Israeli military’s reliance on AWS reflects its embrace in recent years of leading US tech companies to meet the technological demands of war with rapidly scalable storage, computing power and AI-driven services.

The role of AI in Israel’s offensive in Gaza has come under fresh scrutiny particularly after the release of NAZA, a Guardian-produced documentary about the remote surveillance and killing of Palestinian civilians.

The Rolling Stone department is among AWS’s most significant Israeli military clients, documents suggest. Its use of Rekognition in early 2024 to analyse 3.5m images came after it had expanded its use of AWS products and services to store and analyse its data.

Files show the department migrated significant volumes of the data it holds into the so-called “walled garden” in AWS’s cloud throughout 2023. A military source involved in this effort said it had planned to move all of its databases from the military servers into AWS’s cloud.
The source, who spoke on the condition of anonymity, said: “The plan [at Rolling Stone] was to migrate pictures, videos, all the confidential intelligence information – everything.”
A spokesperson for the Israel Defence Forces (IDF) said it “does not intend to comment on engagements or services related to operational needs”.
The Rolling Stone department oversees several expansive databases that collate data on Palestinians, including the system from which the branch takes its name.

Used by the military for decades, the Rolling Stone system is constantly updated and includes data such as basic personal and family details, property holdings, and information on checkpoint crossings, work permits, and criminal activity.

A soldier who provided testimony to Breaking the Silence, an Israeli NGO, in 2016 described Rolling Stone as “a computerised system where all the information relevant to the control of the Palestinian civilian population is centralised”.

As a result of Israel’s control of the population registries covering Gaza and the West Bank, the Rolling Stone department has amassed millions of Palestinians’ photographs taken for the identity cards issued to every resident when they turn 16 years old.

Sources familiar with its work said the images were routinely used for facial recognition programmes. These include Blue Wolf, a smartphone app Israeli soldiers use in the West Bank to scan Palestinians’ faces and access information about them, including whether they’ve been flagged as suspects for arrest.

In Gaza, at temporary Israeli checkpoints established after the ground invasion, cameras trained on Palestinian people were used to capture their images as they approached the sites. Facial recognition was then used to match people to images held in Rolling Stone’s systems, sources said.

The checkpoints became notorious in Gaza as places where people were pulled aside and detained. Many were taken into Israeli custody and held incommunicado, amounting to enforced disappearances, according to several UN bodies and rights groups.

Documents suggest AWS’s cloud technology was used at times during 2024 to support the work of the checkpoints. Military insiders said the checkpoints were referred to by Israeli soldiers as Nakaz – a Hebrew word for drainage.

Harry Davies is one of the Guardian producers on NAZA, which Yuval Abraham co-directed. NAZA is now in cinemas worldwide and will screen for free on the Guardian’s website from early December. Sign up here to be the first to watch it

articles.title: Relocation of Cape Town baboons to sanctuary ignites heated protests
articles.summary: Demonstrators tried to block vehicle carrying the baboons, whose capture authorities say is needed to protect both primate and human
body: The relocation of a troop of baboons in Cape Town to a wildlife sanctuary has triggered furious protests by local people opposed to their capture, which officials argue is necessary to stop human-wildlife conflict in the city.
Related: ‘It’s hard to sell a house when it’s covered in baboon faeces’: Cape Town divided over plan to remove its monkeys

The 44-member Waterfall troop (named after the area they mainly inhabit) was captured in the southern seaside suburb of Simon’s Town on Friday and Saturday. A second, smaller Seaforth troop is also due to be moved.

The growth in both baboon and human populations in Cape Town in recent years has led to increased conflict and more baboons dying as a result. Meanwhile, a heated debate has raged between people who believe that baboons and humans can coexist and those who argue that baboons in urban areas are in danger and in some cases need to be relocated. Some animal rights activists have compared authorities’ baboon management to apartheid.
During Friday’s relocation, outraged protesters tried to stop vehicles taking the baboons away. One person sprayed a fire extinguisher, according to the Daily Maverick, a local news outlet.

After the confrontation, the local Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals branch urged those opposed to the baboons’ capture not to try to stop the vehicles. “Capture and transport are already stressful for the baboons,” it said in a statement. “Delaying their arrival prolongs their time in crates and risks adding to that stress – this is not fair on the baboons.”
It said it remained opposed to the baboon’s relocation, adding: “Our presence did not imply support … our inspectors are present because the animals need someone looking out for them.”

On Sunday, dozens of people sat outside the wildlife centre in a silent protest, some tying flowers to the fence. Baboons from a different troop also gathered at the boundary, calling to the newly captive animals, the Daily Maverick reported.

“We stand together for the Seaforth and Waterfall troops, for their freedom, their dignity and their right to live as wild animals,” Mandy Neal, the administrator of the Save Kogelfontein Baboons Facebook group, posted on Monday, calling for weekly Sunday silent protests. “ Our message is simple: CAPTIVITY IS NOT CONSERVATION.”

The City of Cape Town said in a statement on Sunday that the relocation had been successful, with the baboons being monitored 24/7 after being checked by vets and the females receiving contraceptive implants.

It said: “The Waterfall troop has been relocated due to the severity and persistence of human-baboon conflict in the Simon’s Town urban environment, the limited available natural low-lying habitat, the increasing risk to the baboons’ welfare, and public safety concerns … [and] as a very last resort after other interventions were evaluated and deemed ineffective, and as an alternative to culling.”

Prof Justin O’Riain, a behavioural ecologist at the University of Cape Town, said the baboon management plan had undergone two years of public consultations. “It has thus been disappointing watching members of the public and select NGOs, many which did not engage in the stakeholder process, now compromising the safety and welfare of the baboons and people through violent actions directed at staff and baboons in transit.”

articles.title: Monday briefing: The many stages of the UK-EU relationship – and what’s next
articles.summary: In today’s newsletter: From situationship to a possible makeup, a look at the evolving relationship, and the bloc’s big feelings about the future
body: Good morning. Ahead of the hotly anticipated UK-EU summit this Friday, Andy Burnham is expected to make the reset of our relationship with Europe the pivotal theme of his white-tie speech at the lord mayor’s banquet in London tonight.

The prospect of closer ties – and the possibility of going “all the way” to reversing Brexit – has been met with jubilation and relief in some quarters and vehement opposition in others, while around Westminster and across the media the psychodrama has been spiralling for weeks.

At this point, I’m reminded of that Robert Burns couplet: “O wad some Pow’r the giftie gie us / To see oursels as ithers see us!” What does the EU think about all this? Are they ready to reverse what leading figures have repeatedly described as a colossal act of self-harm? Or are they viewing this latest iteration with bombastic side-eye? I posed these questions to Jennifer Rankin, the Guardian’s Brussels correspondent. First the headlines.

UK news | A woman who alleges she was raped by Russell Brand when she was 16 has waived her right to anonymity to campaign for a staggered age of consent, which would make it illegal for adults over a certain age to have sex with 16- and 17-year-olds.

Youth unemployment | Andy Burnham has pledged to intervene as early as childhood to tackle youth unemployment before a watershed review, promising “a root-and-branch rethink of how we support childhood in the modern world”.

Environment | The strongest El Niño in centuries has added urgency to UN climate talks in Turkey as vulnerable countries face “compounding” crises. In other Cop31 news, queer and gay protesters defied a crackdown on LGBTQ+ rights in Turkey to lead a civil society climate march.

UK news | Two people aged 22 and 23 have died after their car was hit by a BMW being pursued by police. West Yorkshire police said four people had been arrested and appealed for witnesses to come forward.

Air transport | The Trump administration says Friday’s four-hour nationwide Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) ground stop that delayed or cancelled thousands of flight stemmed from routine maintenance. The US transportation secretary, Sean Duffy, blamed prior presidents and Congress for the stoppage.

Ahead of the summit, the pro-Brexit polity has been in broadcast mode: headlines from the past few days include: “Burnham’s plot to rejoin the EU would leave the average UK household £6,500 poorer” (Express); “Taxpayers funding pro-EU university courses” (Sunday Telegraph); “Staggering cost of PM’s EU reset” (Daily Mail).

Stay Out, a new campaign against rejoining the European Union, launched last week. While the guy you really want to hear from right now – David Cameron, the prime minister who lost the 2016 Brexit referendum – has insisted the UK’s problems have nothing to do with its exit from the EU.
Even within the Labour fold, there are rumblings of unease from MPs and unions.

But the one-day summit in Brussels this Friday does not include any formal discussion of rejoining: instead, the EU and UK hope to sign deals on food and drink, emissions trading and the youth experience scheme (a work and study exchange programme).

Still, the mood music is upbeat. Back in September, when Burnham first opened the door to a Brexit reversal, French president Emmanual Macron responded: “welcome back.” while Spanish prime minister Pedro Sánchez said: “Spain would welcome Britain’s return with open arms.”

The enthusiasm is genuine, says Jennifer. Indeed, some European diplomats have told her the technicalities could be wrapped up within a year because the UK remains closely aligned with the bloc in so many areas. “It would be such a vote of confidence in the European project for a country to decide to return after voting to leave”.
Situationship: what’s at stake at this week’s summit?

Though Burnham has predicted “some long nights” of negotiation this week, Jennifer says there’s optimism on each side as the first two deals on food and drink and emissions trading were largely agreed.

There are two sticking points with the youth exchange deal. First, the Home Office wants to limit numbers to the UK to keep migration figures low. Second, there’s disagreement over whether those students would pay UK domestic rates of tuition fees or the international rate, which is four or five times higher for some courses.

The UK is offering concessions on tuition fees if it can join Made in Europe, the EU legislation designed to protect domestic manufacturing from cheap Chinese competition. But the EU says it can’t make a deal on Made in Europe this week, because the law is still at a draft stage.

And here’s where it gets complicated. The European Commission has proposed delaying an agreement on tuition fees for six months, which could allow time to get the UK into Made in Europe, a diplomatic win for Britain. But there’s pushback from member states who want to pin down the UK on tuition fees this week. “This is a real priority for the EU, in almost emotional terms,” Jennifer says. “Lots of EU officials and diplomats studied in the UK, or their children did, and they felt this was one of the big losses of Brexit, that these person-to-person links were being eroded.”
On-again, off-again: what else could get in the way of closer working?

In play at Friday’s summit will also be a future deal on Britain’s return to the EU’s internal electricity market and a joint migration pact, with the UK pushing for access to EU crime databases to tackle the small boats crisis.

Member states are already working hard to smooth things out on the electricity front, to stop it becoming a sticking point. A couple of weeks ago, Jennifer reported on leaders from Germany, Denmark and elsewhere calling for deeper cooperation on clean energy – which she reads as an attempt to head off a row about how much the UK should contribute to EU cohesion funds for the evident privilege of cutting red tape, easing trade and, ultimately, reducing costs.
A similar row over UK contributions scuppered negotiations last year on our entry into a €150bn EU defence fund.

It could also be a challenge for the UK to realign with the EU on farming, after changing to a payment model that puts more emphasis on delivering environmental benefits. And past UK governments have been lukewarm about EU AI regulation, devised post Brexit.
Conscious partnership: will the EU welcome future closeness this week?

I learned long ago there’s no such thing as a stupid question, so I ask mine now: will there be a moment on Friday when Ursula von der Leyen offers the equivalent of Macron’s “welcome back”? Will there be a “just give us six months to sort out the paperwork Andy” vibe?

The European Commission president is, by nature, a cautious politician, Jennifer tells me, so she doesn’t expect anything so specific. “I’m sure she – and António Costa, the European Council president – will get asked about it at the press conference, and they’ll want to send a signal about the UK being welcome to rejoin.”

But behind closed doors, in Brussels and other capitals, what Jennifer hears repeatedly is that it’s up to the UK to decide what it wants. And, while the prospect of Brexiteer Nigel Farage in Downing Street has faded in recent months, there remains a deal of caution about the vicissitudes of UK politics. “Now the Burnham government is exploring the options, but there’s also an awareness that you could have a very different government in a few years’ time,” she says.
It’s not you, it’s me: what else is Europe worrying about?

The EU and its member states are preoccupied with far weightier problems: the war in Ukraine (Volodymyr Zelenskyy attends every EU summit), the rise in support for the far right, street protests, hybrid threats from Russia, a trade deficit with China that has reached a staggering €1bn a day in 2026.
“There are so many other issues crowding on the agenda,” says Jennifer. So it’s not all about us? “That’s actually been the theme of my decade of reporting from Brussels,” she says with a laugh.

There’s profound concern about the prospect of Marine Le Pen winning the French presidential elections next year, which could tip the bloc into a crisis if she pursues her resolutely anti-EU agenda, which includes reducing France’s substantial contribution to the EU budget.

Beyond that, there’s a broader question about increasingly divided and unstable politics across member states. “Every single member state has to agree to the UK’s re-entry,” Jennifer reminds me. “Who knows what the EU will look like in 2030 when Britain could be having a rejoin referendum?”
Tuesday | The former health and social care secretary Alan Milburn’s long-awaited review into why increasing numbers of young people are falling out of work and education, is expected to be released.

Thursday | German chancellor Friedrich Merz, French president Emmanuel Macron and UK prime minister Andy Burnham will be among around 20 heads of state meeting in Berlin to discuss defence funding for Ukraine, and to establish a unified position on future peace negotiations in its war with Russia.
Friday | This marks last day of the world’s biggest annual climate conference, Cop31, in Turkey, with final negotiations taking place.
With a stellar range of interviews, Nadia Khomami is excellent on 2000s pop culture, and how openly horrible it was to women. Poppy Noor, newsletters team
Emma Beddington’s piece on why gen Xer seem to have worse mental and physical health than boomers is a must-read. Poppy

Amelia Gentleman’s report over the weekend on two very different rape trials and what happened in each of them is a difficult read – but enlightening about all of the ways culture has (and has not) changed since Russell Brand’s prominence. Poppy

Football | England risked throwing away a three-goal lead against Spain after Elliot Anderson was sent off, but held on for a thrilling 3-2 win in Madrid, which Thomas Tuchel hailed as a statement result and the best performance of his tenure.
Cricket | Tom Banton’s century led England to emphatic win, with 135 runs, in second ODI amid Australian soap opera.
Rugby union | Tries from Matt Fagerson and Jack Dempsey gave Scotland a 15-12 win against Australia in the Nations Championship at Murrayfield
“PM vows early years interventions will tackle youth joblessness crisis”, is the Guardian’s front page today.
The i Paper leads with “Pressure grows for new consent law to protect teenagers from adult predators”, Metro has “Rethink on the age of consent”, the Sun writes “Brand’s rant from prison”.

The Telegraph says “Johnson: Britain would back Brexit again”, the Express writes “Brexit U-turn means ‘more asylum seekers’”. The Times has “Zero-hours ban to cost billions”, the Mail has “£80,000 a day spent ferrying migrants around”, the Mirror’s splash is “Dying in the dark”, and the FT’s is “Nvidia scandal spurs drive to choke China’s AI chip supply”.
Grand Theft Auto VI: the cultural event of the decade?

This week, after a 13-year wait, gamers will finally get hold of Grand Theft Auto VI, the latest instalment of the most successful console computer game in history. How did a game of stealing cars and shooting strangers become such an enormous cultural phenomenon? The Guardian’s video games editor, Keza MacDonald, traces the history of games by Rockstar, GTA’s creator, and what its most successful product has told us about the US, the setting of all its games so far.
A bit of good news to remind you that the world’s not all bad

Some travellers seek out ancient landmarks when they visit a new place. Hidde Burgmans, from the Netherlands, looks for ancient trees – and he’s created an app of the same name to help people find remarkable old trees around the world, from Malaysian baobabs to the Fortingall yew in Perthshire, Scotland, thought to be an astounding 5,000 years old.

Users can review remarkable old trees around the world, and upload their favourites to the Ancient Trees app. “On Tuesday somebody photographed a tree in Edinburgh. Today, someone in Freiburg,” said Burgmans. “That just makes me happy. I thought it was quite a niche, geeky thing, but apparently more people are interested in ancient trees than I thought.”
Sign up here for a weekly roundup of The Upside, sent to you every Sunday
And finally, the Guardian’s puzzles are here to keep you entertained throughout the day. Until tomorrow.

articles.title: Will Spain’s snap election in November bring a far-right party into government?
articles.summary: Country’s sixth general election in 11 years could lead to far-right role in government for first time since Franco’s death
body: Spaniards head to the polls on 29 November to vote in the country’s sixth general election in 11 years. The snap election could end eight years of socialist-led rule and bring a far-right party into government for the first time since Spain’s return to democracy after the death of Gen Franco.

Pedro Sánchez, Spain’s socialist prime minister, called the snap election on 5 October after the conservative People’s party (PP), the far-right Vox party and the rightwing, pro-independence Catalan party Junts voted down emergency measures the government had put together to tackle a housing crisis.

The lack of affordable housing has become a key electoral issue, triggering large protests across Spain. The issue was thrown into sharp relief by the case of the late Maricarmen Abascal, an 87-year-old woman who was evicted from her home in Madrid because she could not afford the 230% rent increase demanded by the investment fund that had bought her apartment. Last Wednesday more than 3 million people took part in a general strike called in response to soaring housing prices.

Sánchez and his Spanish Socialist Workers’ party (PSOE) are hoping their efforts to address the housing crisis – and the fact their plans were torpedoed by the PP, Vox and Junts – will mobilise progressive voters and deliver them another four-year term.

But it is a risky strategy. All the polls point to the PP finishing first in the election but falling short of an absolute majority. That means it would need to enlist the support of Vox to help it govern. A coalition deal between the PP and Vox would signal the return of the far right to government in Spain for the first time in the country’s post-dictatorship democratic history.
The prime minister, who has a reputation for risk-taking and wrongfooting his opponents, believes the housing crisis could be a winning issue after a turbulent and painful couple of years.

Sánchez’s minority coalition government, with the smaller, leftwing Sumar alliance, has struggled to get legislation through a fraught congress and has not passed a budget since 2023. Junts, which offered him conditional support three years ago, has attempted to extract maximum benefits from the government, only to abandon it when it feels so inclined, as it did with the emergency housing measures.

His government has also been fiercely criticised over its handling of the crisis in Spain’s north African exclave of Ceuta, which was sparked when about 80,000 people crossed into the territory from neighbouring Morocco in the space of 48 hours.

What’s more, Sánchez’s administration, party and inner circle have been mired in corruption allegations over the past two years, which have proved acutely embarrassing for a prime minister who took office vowing to be a scourge of sleaze and graft.

Given all that, Sánchez may have decided that an election campaign harnessing public anger over the housing situation made more political sense than enduring further months of deadlock and bad headlines.

Sánchez’s campaign, in which he has sought to play up his government’s social and economic achievements, has been overshadowed by the high-speed rail crash that killed 69 people on 28 October. The accident, nine months after 46 people died in another rail crash on the same line, has raised questions over the safety and management of Spain’s much-vaunted high-speed rail network. Sánchez’s transport minister, Óscar Puente, bowed to pressure and resigned days after the latest crash, saying: “Neither the country, nor I, can bear 100 deaths in less than a year.”

Alberto Núñez Feijóo, the PP’s leader, has accused the Sánchez administration of failing to keep Spaniards safe, while Vox has lashed out at what it termed the government’s “incompetence, corruption, cronyism and a lack of investment in maintenance and infrastructure improvements”.

Spain’s congress has 350 seats, meaning that any party or coalition of parties needs to win at least 176 seats to secure an outright majority. According to the polls, the PP could win about 130 seats, the PSOE about 110 and Vox about 63.

Barring a far better than expected performance from the PSOE, the PP is set to win, ushering in the prospect of a deal with Vox. The PP, which six years ago repudiated its far-right rival as a party that practised a politics based on “fear, anger, resentment and revenge”, has since adopted a far friendlier tone towards Vox, its anti-immigrant policies and its talk of “remigration”. The PP and Vox already jointly govern four Spanish regions, so the precedent for deals between the two parties has been set.

Sánchez has billed the election as a stark choice between his progressive government and a Spanish right that would abandon hard-won social advances. “You, the men and women of Spain, must decide whether you want to join the far-right wave that rolls back progress wherever it governs, or to ensure that Spain remains a bastion of openness, social justice and environmental responsibility,” he said as he announced the snap vote.

The small parties to the left of the PSOE – including its former partners in Sumar – are unlikely to attract enough votes to help the socialists form another coalition government. The Broad Front, led by the former Barcelona mayor Ada Colau, has united many of the leftwing groupings, but Podemos has declined to join them. Between them, the Broad Front and Podemos are forecast to win about 13 seats, leaving them and the PSOE far short of a majority.

Sánchez’s opponents are seeking to portray the election as a referendum on the style of self-serving politics they disdainfully refer to as sanchismo. Feijóo has promised “a return to decency as a basic principle” if his party wins on 29 November.

Its leader, Santiago Abascal, has said his party stands for “putting nationals first, deregulation, tax relief, and the return of those who should not be in Spain”. One of Vox’s main policies is “national priority”, or giving Spaniards precedence over those from overseas when it comes to accessing subsidised housing, social rentals, grants and benefits.
Despite agreeing to “national priority” in the regions it already governs with Vox, the PP has said the policy must obey Spanish and European law.

Feijóo told El País last week: “National priority is based on rootedness in Spain, not nationality, and on respect for the constitution and European treaties. Nothing can be agreed that falls outside the constitution or those treaties.”

In July last year, Vox floated the idea of deporting up to 8 million people of foreign origin – including the children of immigrants – arguing that “it’s very difficult for them to get used to our customs”.

The party later backtracked on the “remigration” plan, and has since said it would apply only to those who enter Spain illegally, who commit crimes or who “come to Spain to live off welfare benefits”.
Abascal argues that the policies are “not at all driven by hatred toward those from outside, but rather by love for those on the inside”.

articles.title: Ukraine war briefing: Energy attacks made possible by continuing Starshield restrictions, says Zelenskyy
articles.summary: The president reiterated criticisms he made last week – saying Ukraine’s use of Elon Musk’s satellite-based service continued to face restrictions. What we know on day 1,727
body: Attacks on Ukrainian energy and railway infrastructure were being made possible ⁠partly due to restrictions on Ukraine’s use of Elon Musk’s Starshield service, Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Sunday – reiterating criticism he made late last week. “Many of these ‌strikes are getting through because restrictions on the speed of Starshield terminals along the frontline in the temporarily occupied territories are still there.” The president said Russian forces were singling out ​specific regions – in particular, southeastern Dnipropetrovsk and Zaporizhzhia – and repeatedly striking them over several days. There have ​been many outages, and restoration ​is proceeding,” he ‌said. “Power has ​been ​restored to some extent, but there is still a lot of work ahead.”

Zelenskyy made similar comments about the Starshield satellite system on Friday accusing SpaceX of not telling the truth over restrictions on Ukraine’s use of the system, saying the decision to impose speed limits appeared to be “political” rather than “technical”. As a result, incoming jet-powered Russian Shahed drones could no longer be intercepted, and Ukraine’s own mid-range strikes against military targets in Russian-occupied territory were also severely affected, he said.

Zelenskyy also announced on Sunday that a meeting of Kyiv’s allies, the so-called Coalition of the Willing, was being prepared, aimed at defining the European position in talks on ending the war with Russia. He said a meeting of the Ramstein group – countries helping to support Ukraine’s defence – was set for next week and that it needs to “send a strong signal to Russia that Ukraine will not be left without support”. Europe has chosen five countries – France, Britain, Poland, Germany and Italy – to send representatives to future Ukraine peace talks. “It is an important meeting, and it could be a historic one,” Zelenskyy said in his daily evening address.

Cross-border attacks have continued with Ukraine striking⁠ ⁠the bridge linking ​Russia ⁠and Crimea across ⁠the ​Kerch ‌strait, ‌causing traffic to ‌be halted, the peninsula’s Russian-backed ‌governor, Sergei Aksyonov, said ​on ​Telegram on Monday. On Sunday, a Russian strike on Chornomorsk injured six people and damaged energy infrastructure, leaving about 41,000 customers without power. Russia struck energy and railway infrastructure in eight regions of ⁠Ukraine overnight, said Zelenskyy.

Estonia will close all its border crossings with Russia from 1 December after a suspected sabotage attack on a drone maker in the Baltic state over the weekend, which authorities said was ordered by Russia’s GRU military intelligence service. The Estonian prime minister, Kristen Michal, linked the attacks with Estonia’s continuing support for Ukraine. “Russia’s aim is to make us afraid, make us hesitate and weaken our support for Ukraine,” Michal said. Russian ⁠Foreign Ministry spokesperson Maria Zakharova was quoted on ​Sunday saying any closure of the border by Estonia would ​be another demonstration of “Russophobia”.

Warnings from Russia to western diplomats to leave Kyiv or risk being killed were “cognitive warfare”, say European ambassadors, some of whom have spoken to the Guardian’s Luke Harding about why they chose to stay in Ukraine during the war. The EU’s ambassador in Kyiv, Katarína Mathernová, said the threats were part of Vladimir Putin’s strategic goal to destroy the EU. But ambassadors say their continued presence sends a powerful signal of solidarity to Ukraine’s embattled leadership.

Prince Harry made a surprise visit to Ukraine over the weekend, meeting wounded veterans and medics specialising in war injuries and telling them: “You’re going to win the war.” In his fourth visit since the war began and his second time in Lviv, he met patients and staff at an orthopaedic clinic treating wounded military personnel and civilians. “We’ve invested in them before they put the uniform on and we must invest with them once the uniform comes off,” he said.

articles.title: ‘The blood of these brothers cries out’: Pope Leo demands justice for people killed protecting the Amazon
articles.summary: Pontiff delivers forceful speech in Peru as he travels from high in the Andes into the Amazon
body: Pope Leo XIV has demanded justice for environmental defenders killed for protecting the Amazon and backed efforts by Indigenous peoples to stop their lands from being ravaged by logging and illegal mining.

On the penultimate day of his South American tour, Leo on Sunday travelled into the Peruvian Amazon and channelled one of Pope Francis’s core teachings that links care for the most vulnerable with care for God’s creation.
“The cry of the Earth and the cry of the poor are inseparable,” Leo told Indigenous representatives and missionaries gathered along the Ucayali River in the north-eastern city of Pucallpa.
Related: Pope Leo gets rapturous welcome on return to Peru: ‘This visit is like a big party’

He said he came to Pucallpa to support them in their search for justice and peace and referred to what environmental groups estimate have been 57 murders of environmental defenders between 2010 and 2024.
“The blood of these brothers cries out to God and demands justice,” Leo said to applause from the crowd, many of whom were wearing traditional feathered headwear and face markings of the region.

In addition to deforestation, illegal gold mining has become an increasingly lucrative business in the Amazon, devastating forests and polluting rivers. Illegal mining and coca production has also driven deforestation.

Leo addressed the combination of threats in one of his most forceful speeches to date, drawing on his years of experience as a Peruvian bishop and Francis’s constant preaching about the environment and the plight of Indigenous groups.

During the encounter and a subsequent mass in Pucallpa, he demanded a different model of economic development that respects the Earth and the Indigenous peoples who care for it, rather than the “irresponsible exploitation” by outside actors.

“Very little has been done – and very slowly at that – while the means to exploit and pollute creation have accelerated,” he said at mass. “In the face of these evils, let us not bury the Lord’s gifts, for he gives us the strength to repair and heal the suffering caused by an insatiable thirst for domination.”
In Peru, most murders of environmental defenders go unpunished; only a few have resulted in convictions.

The most recent conviction came in the case of Kichwa leader Quinto Inuma Alvarado, who was murdered in 2023 when he was ambushed by hitmen on a river in the San Martín region, the Amazonian territory he was defending.
Leo also referred to a notorious rise in sexual violence against Indigenous Awajún and Wampis schoolgirls in the northern Amazon, and blasted the “impunity” and “corruption” surrounding them.
The Awajún and Wampis Women’s Council has recorded 370 cases of sexual violence in the Condorcanqui province between January and July.
Julio Cusurichi, an Indigenous leader, handed Leo a letter during his visit to Pucallpa, asking him to help protect the rights of uncontacted Indigenous relatives.
“The Peruvian state is weakening the mechanisms that should safeguard their territories,” said the letter from the Indigenous rights organisation Aidesep, on which Cusurichi is a board member.

“We cannot allow economic interests to take precedence over the lives and rights of these vulnerable peoples. Therefore, we ask Pope Leo XIV to raise his voice and support this urgent call for their defence.”

Cardinal Pedro Barreto praised the pope’s decision to meet with Indigenous peoples. Barreto, a former Peruvian archbishop who helped win a multimillion-dollar pollution payout for an Andean town, said: “[Leo] is well aware of all the historical suffering … corruption, illegal mining, deforestation, and the contempt shown by politicians.”

Luis E Fernandez, co-founder of Cincia, a scientific research centre in Peru, also hailed the pontiff’s power to raise awareness. “Pope Leo’s recognition of pollution from illegal mining brings much-needed attention to a crisis affecting Indigenous and riverine communities across the Amazon,” he said.
Fernandez visited the Vatican in September and presented Leo with scientific evidence detailing the impact of illegal gold mining and associated mercury poisoning.
Fernandez visited the Vatican in October and presented Leo with scientific evidence detailing the impact of illegal gold mining and associated mercury poisoning.

Leo’s last full day in Peru was also his most ambitious, crisscrossing the nation to minister to communities high in the Andes mountains. Peru’s air force released footage of the pope inside a helicopter and said it was “an unforgettable memory” to take Leo around the country.
His first stop was the mountain city of Cusco, where huge crowds greeted him.

“It is all worth it,” said Margarida Salomon, 63, who said she came from Sucre in Bolivia to see the pontiff, spending about $500 to take a bus and sleep in a tent. “I am still getting to know this pope, but the fact he is here in the Andes means a lot.”

The visit to Cusco, 3,400m (more than 11,000ft) above sea level, tested Leo’s stamina as he continues recovering from lung cancer surgery last month. Leo sat in the chair of his popemobile during part of the ride around Cusco, but it wasn’t clear if that was to preserve his energy or to steady himself on the uneven streets.
In general, the 71-year-old Leo has seemed unfazed by the toll of the three-nation South American trip, the longest of his pontificate.

articles.title: Women prosecuted for abortions hail ‘historic day’ after receiving pardon
articles.summary: Calls for government to issue formal apology to those investigated after ending pregnancies in England and Wales
body: Campaigners and women previously convicted of illegal abortions have hailed a “historic day” after the pardoning of every woman who has faced criminal investigation for ending a pregnancy during the last 150 years.

A vote in the House of Lords earlier this year introduced legislation to pardon women accused of terminating their own pregnancies outside the legal framework and expunge their criminal records, under section 242 of the Crime and Policing Act 2026, which takes effect on Monday.

The House of Commons had previously voted to amend the laws around abortion to prevent future cases of women being criminalised for ending their own pregnancies, while keeping the legal framework for terminations in place.

However, some women have said that while they are “grateful” for the pardon, they would also like a formal apology from the government, as “none of us should have been on trial, investigated or sent to prison”.
It is understood that the pardons will apply to about 150 women, who have been identified from police records.

Details of convictions, cautions, arrests and police investigations relating to terminations will now be deleted from the women’s records, allowing them to work and travel without restrictions once more.
Several women were prosecuted after ordering medication online or obtaining drugs after a remote consultation, including during the Covid-19 pandemic, to terminate their pregnancies.
Related: Nine in 10 UK voters across parties support right to abortion, poll finds

Some have spoken publicly about not realising they were beyond 24 weeks at the time including Nicola Packer, who was cleared by a jury at Isleworth crown court in London last year after an almost five-year ordeal.
She was prosecuted after she obtained pills from an authorised provider at the height of the pandemic, and had not realised that her pregnancy was more advanced than she initially thought.

Some of the women who have advocated for a change in the law were victims of domestic abuse or coercive control, including Laura*, a young mother who was jailed after her abusive partner coerced her into obtaining pills online.

“We’ve all been through so much to get here,” Packer said. “Although it can’t erase the memories of what we’ve experienced, it does remove the records that have made it difficult for some of us to get and keep jobs, and live our lives.”

“And it further validates the feeling that none of us should have been on trial, investigated or sent to prison,” she added. “It’s a great day for us and I feel lighter knowing that the records have been expunged.”

Amy* said she was “grateful” for the pardon, though it did not “undo the years of stigma, distress and judgment”. She said women had their parenting questioned, faced restrictions on contact with their own children and were seen as “a serious danger to society”.

“I do believe women deserved an apology for what they went through,” she said. “Although the authorities may have been acting within the law at the time, we have to remember that for many women, particularly during Covid, there was isolation, fear and nowhere to turn.
“Women were dealing with incredibly difficult circumstances, often without the support or help they needed.”
She added: “For me, the hardest part is knowing that I will always carry this experience with me. The publicity surrounding my case meant that my identity and where I lived became public knowledge.

“People know who I am and where I live, and even now I can struggle to walk into my local community without feeling that people are looking at me or judging me. Having a pardon doesn’t take away those experiences or give me back the privacy I lost.”

Up until the recent law change, women were often prosecuted under Victorian legislation dating back to 1861. They include Fanny Warboys, who was criminalised a year later, in 1862, a widow who ended up injured after a backstreet abortion and was sentenced to three months in prison.
Another woman, Mary Jane Baynon, 32, was jailed for three months in 1891 after travelling to London from her home in Sligo in western Ireland, and being reported to police by a fake surgeon.

In an early example of judges showing compassion for women who found themselves before the courts, Emma Sarah Rice, 25, was found guilty of an illegal abortion, but was sentenced to just one day without hard labour in 1881. She was still pregnant and in ill health, and “his Lordship said he thought the woman was more to be pitied than condemned”.

Dr Alison Wright, the president of the Royal College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists (RCOG), said the pardons recognised “the injustice of historical convictions” and she was “delighted to see this progress”.

Dr Jonathan Lord, the co-chair of the RCOG’s abortion taskforce, welcomed a “historic day”, when “for the first time since the 13th century, women who have been convicted after a pregnancy loss for an alleged abortion will no longer have to carry the consequences of a criminal record”.
Many of the women prosecuted had no other convictions or cautions, but found themselves unable to work in certain jobs because they had been arrested for abortion offences.

Others found themselves having to disclose traumatic medical events to potential employers, even though they were never charged with a crime, as their arrests had shown on enhanced Disclosure and Barring Service checks.

Heidi Stewart, the chief executive of the British Pregnancy Advisory Service (BPAS), said: “For too long, women have faced the devastating consequences of outdated abortion laws … While no pardon can undo the distress and trauma these women have experienced, this historic change in the law recognises the profound harm caused by their criminalisation and represents a meaningful step towards justice.”

Women affected do not need to apply to have their convictions removed, or take any action, as police forces and courts will begin updating records in line with new requirements, which the government has described as “a priority”.

Alex Davies-Jones, the minister for victims and tackling violence against women and girls, said: “Pardoning women for abortion offences related to their own pregnancy has been a priority and I’m pleased to be able to commence the change that parliament voted for.

“For those affected, I know that clear and accessible information about what happens next is vital. Women do not have to take any direct action themselves, but can find out more information online and contact our dedicated casework team.”

articles.title: Australia, UK, Canada and Italy urge Israel to allow critical aid to Gaza ahead of winter
articles.summary: Four countries call situation ‘entirely reversible’ in joint statement as flooding exacerbates humanitarian crisis
body: Australia, Canada, the United Kingdom and Italy have urged Israel to allow critical humanitarian aid to enter Gaza, describing the situation on the ground as “dire”.

The four nations released a joint statement on Monday urging Israel to allow 150,000 tents and other vital supplies being held at the border into Gaza ahead of winter, describing the situation on the ground as “dire”.
“We, the foreign ministers of Australia, Canada, Italy and the United Kingdom, are clear that as winter takes hold in Gaza, the humanitarian situation on the ground is dire,” the statement said.
“The recent floods have brought further suffering – and this was only the first storm of the winter. People in Gaza desperately need shelter and humanitarian assistance.”
In Australia, Labor backbencher Ed Husic dismissed the joint call, warning his own government couldn’t “statement our way out of this”.

Husic, a former cabinet minister and vocal critic of Israel, told News24: “My view, like a lot of people in the Australian public, is that when you see vulnerable people, especially kids, that are being targeted in horrific ways, that we can’t stand by and literally say we’ll statement our way out of this.”

“When the history is written about our government, this will be one of those things … we should have done different. If there is a chapter in that book that talks about the things we should have done differently … this will be a case in point.”
Husic has previously called for Australia to take more concrete action against Israel including further sanctions.
Related: Lewis Hamilton says ‘Israel’s genocide in Gaza is appalling’ after Rafah visit
The four foreign ministers said Israel had time to act “before the winter fully sets in”.

“This situation is entirely reversible … we today urge the government of Israel to stop the delays now and allow immediate, rapid and unimpeded humanitarian access throughout Gaza,” the foreign ministers said.
“The crossings must be opened, and the tents allowed in. Dual-use items necessary for humanitarian operations and early recovery must be granted entry before it is too late.”

Tens of thousands of Palestinians in Gaza have been left in waterlogged and damaged tents after deadly storms in the past week. Thousands more have been left without shelter while sanitation infrastructure has also been destroyed by storms.
At least four Palestinian children and a woman were killed as heavy rains and wind battered fragile, leaky tents.

A spokesperson for the foreign minister said in response to Husic’s comments that the Albanese government had “taken concrete action”, including imposing sanctions on senior Israeli ministers and providing more than $100 million in humanitarian assistance to civilians in Gaza.
“We will continue to pursue further targeted measures in coordination with international partners to deter illegal settlements and settler violence.”

Australia’s Greens leader and foreign affairs spokesperson, David Shoebridge, said “harsh words” from the government would do little and that Labor should instead take concrete action. He was critical of the government’s previous decision not to join allies to implement an import ban on trade from illegal Israeli settlements.

“The Israeli government has not responded to harsh words from Australia before, they won’t now. Material action, sanctions on the war cabinet, ending the two-way arms trade, implementing sanctions on illegal settlements as other nations have done. These are real actions the Albanese government can take but has failed to,” Shoebridge said.

Nasser Mashni, the president of the Australia Palestine Advocacy Network, also said the criticism from Australia and other countries should be followed by action against Israel, including further sanctions and a two-way arms embargo.
“As we enter the fourth year of Israel’s genocide in Gaza, Israel deliberately continues to make Palestinians suffer,” Mashni said.

“Palestinian families are struggling to keep their children warm in flood-soaked tents while Israel continues to obstruct humanitarian aid. Penny Wong’s expressions of concern are meaningless without concrete action. International law demands action, not more empty words.”

The group of foreign ministers urged all parties to implement the comprehensive plan for Gaza, respect the ceasefire and “their obligations under international humanitarian law” and allow “aid to reach the people who need it”.
The Israeli embassy in Australia said Israel “continues to facilitate extensive humanitarian assistance to Gaza” including shelter, food, water and medical supplies.
“Israel continues to work with international organisations and donor countries to facilitate further assistance,” the embassy said.

“More than 820 requests covering tens of thousands of trucks carrying winter-related supplies have been approved, although many have yet to be brought into Gaza by the organisations responsible for their delivery.”

articles.title: Estonia to close all border crossings with Russia after attack on drone maker
articles.summary: Authorities say Russian intelligence service ordered attack which Estonian PM links to Tallinn’s support for Ukraine
body: Estonia will close all its border crossings with Russia from 1 December after a suspected sabotage attack on a drone maker in the Baltic state over the weekend, which authorities said was ordered by Russia’s GRU military intelligence service.

On Saturday morning, eight people were detained during an attempted attack on Threod Systems, a defence company that manufactures long-range attack and reconnaissance drones. No injuries or damage were reported after the company’s security team responded to the incident.

Estonia’s internal security service, Kapo, said on Sunday the attack was carried out “with the aim of causing an explosion and setting the building on fire”. Authorities have requested a court order for five of those detained to remain in custody, Estonia’s public broadcaster ERR reported.

The Estonian prime minister, Kristen Michal, said the border closure was needed to reduce the risk of further attacks and “send a clear message that attacks on Estonia’s defence industry and defence capabilities” were unacceptable.
He linked the attacks with Estonia’s continuing support for Ukraine. “Russia’s aim is to make us afraid, make us hesitate and weaken our support for Ukraine,” Michal said.
“Estonia’s response is the opposite. We will strengthen our security, work even more closely with businesses and our allies, increase pressure on Russia and continue supporting Ukraine.”

The Estonian foreign minister, Margus Tsahkna, echoed the warning, saying: “Russia must understand that hostile actions against Estonia come with consequences. Attempts to intimidate, destabilise or undermine our security will not go unanswered.”
Estonia operates three border crossings with Russia – Narva in the north, and Koidula and Luhamaa in the south. The authorities did not specify how long the closure would be.
It is the second attempted attack on an Estonian defence company that authorities have attributed to Russia, after an arson attack at Milrem Robotics in August.
Related: Estonia blames Russia for arson attack on drone maker supplying Ukraine
In September, Kapo said it was confident that the incident was “a deliberate and pre-planned attack carried out on behalf of Russian special services”.
The agency also said it fitted a pattern of Russian attacks targeting defence and drone companies, particularly those with links to Ukraine.

At the time Estonia summoned Russia’s chargé d’affaires over the attack, but the Kremlin denied any link to Russia, saying it was a “baseless” and “ill-considered” accusation “with absolutely no relation to reality”.

Several European intelligence services have repeatedly warned of potential attacks on defence companies and growing Russian attempts to recruit citizens in EU and Nato countries – on online messaging platforms – to carry out acts of sabotage.

Michal noted that the weekend’s arrests came after security agencies told the defence industry of potential risks. “We do not warn about these threats without reason. Preparedness matters, and this time it clearly paid off,” he said.

The Russian foreign ministry spokesperson, Maria Zakharova, told state news agency Tass: “If ‌these [border closures] are ‌their real plans, then ‌they fit into yet another bout of aggressive and unrestrained Russophobia.”

articles.title: ‘If you don’t shower, so what?’ The western diplomats staying put in under-attack Kyiv
articles.summary: Ambassadors say presence sends powerful signal of solidarity and support amid escalation in Russian strikes and warnings
body: The warning from Moscow was blunt. Western diplomats should immediately leave the Ukrainian capital, Kyiv. If they failed to do so they would be “in mortal danger”. The statement added that Russia would not be responsible for any “potential negative consequences” if its advice was ignored.

European envoys in Kyiv responded to the Kremlin’s threat last month with a loud raspberry. Denmark’s ambassador to Ukraine, Thomas Lund-Sørensen, took to social media to say that he was staying. So did the ambassadors from Germany, Italy, Spain, Sweden, France, Poland and Estonia. Even the Americans indicated they would not be budging.

Speaking at his embassy office, decorated with a Lego Cossack warrior, Lund-Sørensen said the Russians were trying to spook Europeans in order to undermine support for Ukraine. “It’s cognitive warfare. These attacks have been going on for a long time. They are trying to influence public opinion in my country. Of course we will continue here,” he said.

The ambassador admitted that his job had scary moments, shared by all in Kyiv. “If you don’t find it frightening when 10 ballistic missiles hit within a couple of minutes you should probably go and see someone,” he said, but added: “There is a difference between being in uncomfortable and life-threatening situations. If you don’t shower, so what?”

The decision to remain in a city under fire is not without risk. On Friday, a drone crashed into a hospital in central Kyiv, the institute for orthopaedics and traumatology, a few hundred metres from Lund-Sørensen’s workplace. The bang could be heard for miles around.

Russia has dramatically stepped up its attacks since August, hurling missiles and hundreds of jet-powered drones. Major urban centres such as Kharkiv and Odesa have suffered, too. Seemingly frustrated by failure to progress on the battlefield, the Kremlin has intensified its all-out campaign against civilians.

It has targeted bridges across the Dnipro river, thermal heating plants and substations, as well as trains and railway stations. Power cuts last most of the day. In the past week, there was no water for 24 hours. The bombing has reached the historic centre of Kyiv, where many embassies are located. A strike in September hit a building a couple of hundred metres from the German embassy. In October 2022, the embassy’s visa office was damaged in an attack that killed eight people.

In 2025, two missiles landed in the car park next to the EU delegation building. Deadly metal cubes perforated its ground floor, shattering armoured windows. The strike was at dawn, before staff arrived. Nobody was hurt. This September, a drone exploded 500 metres away. Debris ravaged the ninth-floor, bringing down glass, ceiling panels and the ventilation system.

“I was in a meeting with seven colleagues. We ran to the corridor,” said Katarína Mathernová, the EU’s ambassador in Kyiv. “I’ve never heard anything that loud in my life. There were plumes of smoke. It was shocking.” The delegation is now reinforcing its outer walls with sandbags. It has put beanbags in corridors, for staff to use during air raids. There are foldable beds and extra showers.

Asked whether the Kremlin wanted to murder diplomats, as opposed to merely scaring them a little, Mathernová replied with a quote from Catch 22, Joseph Heller’s famous satirical novel. “As Yossarian says: ‘They are trying to kill me! They are lobbing bombs at us!’ I think they are warning shots. They [the Russians] are more and more brazen and callous.”

Vladimir Putin’s strategic goal, she added, was to destroy the EU. She described Russia’s latest threat as “intimidation”, made in the hope that some diplomats from the global south might abandon Kyiv. Meanwhile, the city was creaking. “The level of attacks are much higher than last year, and the power cuts earlier. We’ve had no water in our building. The soft underbelly of a modern city is its sewage system,” she said.

As the capital braces for winter, ambassadors say their continued presence sends a powerful signal of solidarity to Ukraine’s embattled leadership. “They tell us thank you for being here,” Lund-Sørensen said. A fellow ambassador added: “We would all like to stay. We feel conscious that our presence is politically and psychologically important for Ukraine and its resilience.”

The envoy said that in his view the Russians were not hitting foreign missions “by design”. He thought, however, that “sooner or later” a diplomat would be killed by a drone “falling in the wrong place” – an act that would plunge that country’s government into crisis, as it mulled how to respond to Putin’s violence and disregard for international law.

For visiting prime ministers and presidents, getting to and from Kyiv has become more dangerous. The capital’s airport has been shut since the 2022 invasion. Train or car are the only options. On a recent journey from Poland, the envoy said he had to leave his rail compartment twice because of marauding drones. “I sat in the woods for one and a half hours. The train staff gave me a biscuit,” he said.

Frequent air alerts and attacks on bridges have disrupted embassy business and made it difficult for local Ukrainian staff to get to work, he added. The envoy acknowledged: “I have a privileged existence. An alarm goes off and I go and sleep in the basement. Ukrainians have adapted their security protocols. But it’s more inconvenient. There’s a degree of nervousness.”

Mathernová said she sleeps on a mattress in the bathroom of her hotel suite during Russian strikes. She pointed out that millions of Ukrainians are forced to do the same thing – kipping down in bomb shelters, corridors and on the cold floors of metro stations. “There is nothing funny about using winter as a weapon of mass destruction,” she posted earlier this year, after a Kremlin official mocked a photo of her in pyjamas.

Kyiv is classified as a hardship role. Western ambassadors typically stay for two years, separated from families. Lund-Sørensen said there was not exactly “a queue” of colleagues wanting to work in Ukraine but enough “right people” volunteered. “It’s really hard to imagine as a diplomat a more meaningful posting than Ukraine. Its struggle against Russia is personal to me and my country,” he said.

At weekends the envoy relaxes by going on long cycle rides. Mathernová said she enjoyed Nordic walking in the botanical gardens, as well as saunas and dinners with friends. “Kyiv has an unbelievable array of amazing restaurants. One of the things I will miss most is its culinary scene. And it’s can-do attitude. Everything is possible. It’s a big contrast with Brussels,” she said.
Luke Harding’s Betrayal: Trump, Putin and the New Age of Conquest is published by Guardian Faber. To support the Guardian, order your copy at guardianbookshop.com Delivery charges may apply

articles.title: Hundreds of thousands of Czechs protest in Prague over media freedom
articles.summary: Estimated 350,000 people rally against plan to scrap licence fees and fund broadcasters from state budget
body: Hundreds of thousands of Czechs have rallied in Prague to protest against a perceived government attempt to stifle media freedom.

The gathering on Sunday to save the mandatory licence fees that fund Czechia’s public broadcasters drew more than 350,000 people, making it one of the biggest in the country’s history, organisers said.

Many people wore triangular paper hats similar to an animated TV character called Večerníček, a children’s bedtime story mascot who has become a symbol of the protest. Others carried banners saying: “We won’t give media away.”
The event was held at the capital’s Letná Plain, the cradle of the 1989 Velvet Revolution which ended more than 40 years of communist rule in the country.

It marked the latest challenge to the prime minister, Andrej Babiš, and his coalition of populist, hard-right nationalist and Eurosceptic parties, and follows weeks of demonstrations in towns and cities and a strike by staff at Czech TV and Czech Radio.
Related: Public media freedom has been eroded across central Europe. Now Czechs are rallying to protect theirs

Protesters say the plan to scrap licence fees and fund the broadcasters from the state budget would give ministers more leverage over newsrooms and follows the example of Hungary, Poland, Serbia and Slovakia, where current and previous rightwing populist governments eroded media independence.
A series of protests has been held since late October, when the first reading of the bill to scrap the licence fees was pushed through in the middle of the night.

The Million Moments for Democracy group, which organised the demonstration, said the authorities would now grasp the level of opposition. “We do witness here something extraordinary today,” said Mikuláš Minář, the lead organiser. “It’s just a beginning.”

In a statement, the group demanded that the government withdraw its plan and expressed concern that Babiš and his coalition partners posed a threat to democracy. “Babiš and his government obviously think they will get away with anything … that they can ignore experts, silence critics and treat democratic institutions like their property,” the group said.
“We refuse the Slovak scenario,” said one protest banner. “Hands off the media,” said another.

Šárka Dumišincová, a singer, said for her the media represented freedom. “The fact that someone here is trying to control that freedom is unacceptable to me. That’s why I’m here today,” she told the Associated Press.
“We need to keep media independent. The government is taking steps to control them, cut their funding and affect what they broadcast,” computer programmer Jan Snasel told AFP at the rally.
The proposed changes, which would cut state television and radio budgets by about 15%, have drawn fire from international media organisations.

The European Broadcasting Union, the European Federation of Journalists, Reporters Without Borders and the International Press Institute have also criticised the government’s media plan, likening it to controversial moves by Slovakia’s prime minister, Robert Fico, and Hungary’s former premier Viktor Orbán.
Babiš, a billionaire who returned to power last year, said protesters were riling up the public with unfounded claims about threats to media freedom.
Last week, he published an op-ed on what he called the “seven lies” being peddled by the opposition over the licence fees, which together add up to 205 koruna (£7) a month.

“Anyone who talks about ‘nationalisation’ [of public media] is deliberately lying,” he wrote, describing the criticism as “hysterical outbursts”. “Under no circumstances will we interfere in editorial work.”

Babiš heads a coalition that includes his ANO, or YES, movement, the rightwing Motorists for Themselves and the anti-migrant and pro-Russian Freedom and Direct Democracy party. Despite the protests, ANO still enjoys the backing of about 30% in opinion polls.

articles.title: Iran launches drone attacks against US military base in Bahrain
articles.summary: Strikes cast further doubt on peace talks between Tehran and Washington with increasing risk of escalation
body: Iran has launched drone attacks against a US military base in Bahrain, casting further doubt on peace talks between Tehran and Washington and raising the spectre of escalation.
Blasts sounded over the Gulf nation on Sunday in the second Iranian drone attack in three days in retaliation for US strikes in Iran.

Meanwhile, in Yemen, Iran’s Houthi allies advanced against pro-government forces in the south, opening a potential route to Aden. Iran also claimed that a mine sank an oil supertanker in the strait of Hormuz.
The developments deepened gloom about the chances of any diplomatic breakthrough in the region.

Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps said they launched six drones targeting a US air defence radar at the Al-Rifaa helicopter base in retaliation for “hostile US actions”. Authorities in Bahrain said air defences intercepted the drones before they reached their targets.

At a press conference in Tehran the foreign ministry spokesperson, Esmaeil Baghaei, said Iran would continue to respond to any military aggression by the US or other states. Asked if the latest strikes indicated a change in Iranian direction as negotiations with the US have stalled, he said Iran was “not waiting for anyone” and was focused on its security.
US forces have conducted a series of strikes against Iranian targets in recent weeks, including Qeshm Island in the strait of Hormuz.
Donald Trump last week called them minor strikes and said Saudi Arabia and other Gulf states had cautioned him against large-scale combat operations.

However, the president also said Washington was no longer seeking a deal with Iran and that he had instructed the vice-president, JD Vance, to switch his focus to alleged corruption and fraud in Democrat-run cities and states.
Vance – who blamed the Republicans’ loss of Congress in midterm elections on the Iran war – had requested a personal meeting with Iranian negotiators to discuss peace terms.
A conflict that began with joint US and Israeli attacks against Iran in February remains at an impasse, with the US maintaining a naval blockade and Iran its chokehold over the strait of Hormuz.

In a separate development, Iran’s Revolutionary Guards claimed that two ships hit mines in the strait of Hormuz and that one, an oil supertanker with 2m barrels of oil, sank. The ships suffered “massive explosions and fire”, said the statement.
There was no immediate independent verification. The US military recently claimed it had cleared all mines from main routes through the waterway.
The strikes against Bahrain suggested Iran has decided on a tit-for-tat response to US attacks.

Bahrain hosts significant US bases, including a forward base that was home to the US Fifth Fleet and US Naval Forces Central Command, operating as a central support hub for military operations in the Middle East.

Tehran repeatedly targeted the kingdom until September, when there was a lull in attacks. That ended on Friday when Iran launched drones against a US radar facility. US Central Command said it shot down two drones without any injury or damage.
The attacks on Sunday prompted sirens and alerts from Bahrain’s authorities urging residents to seek shelter.
“It’s exactly what I was hoping wouldn’t happen: Iranian attacks starting again, with all the worry and uncertainty that go with them,” resident Hayat Ibrahim, 65, told Agence France Presse.
Bahrain’s foreign ministry called the resumption of attacks “heinous aggression” and a flagrant violation of international law.

The kingdom rejected Tehran’s “flimsy pretexts and baseless claims” to target its territory, it said in a statement. “The kingdom also rejects the transformation of its territory into an arena for settling scores and holds Iran fully responsible for these attacks and their consequences.”
Jordan, Egypt, Saudi Arabia, and Qatar condemned the attacks and expressed solidarity with Bahrain.

In Yemen, Saudi Arabia’s campaign against the Iranian-aligned Houthi rebels reeled when forces fighting on behalf of the Yemeni government retreated from the Bab el-Mandeb strait to defend ⁠Aden on the southern ​coast.

“The Southern Armed Forces announce the implementation of ‌a redeployment operation for its forces from Dhubab Airport and the Bab el-Mandeb area, west of Taiz Governorate,” the main military force fighting for Yemen’s government in the south said in a statement.
The admission signalled the apparent failure of a six-week government counteroffensive to drive the Houthis from the mouth of the Red Sea to secure a key oil route.
A Houthi missile strike near Aden killed people and wounded 12 near Aden, AFP reported, citing military and government sources.
• Additional reporting by Agence France Presse and Associated Press

articles.title: Chickens are great characters, not cowards
articles.summary: Letter: Jo Barlow kept chickens for more than 15 years and found them to be intelligent, brave and funny
body: Whoever deemed chickens synonymous with cowardice obviously didn’t tell my 14-year‑old bantam who took on a hungry Harris hawk and won (Chickens are synonymous with cowardice. Is it time to stick up for our feathered friends?, 11 November).
I kept chickens for more than 15 years and found them to be intelligent, unique characters who could be brave, funny, naughty, loving and kind in equal measure.

They display a wide range of emotions, including empathy for members of their flock that were ill, and grief at their passing. They also took great delight in terrorising my cats and stealing food from the plates of small children.

Branding chicken-kind broadly as cowardly removes their individuality and, as with labelling foxes as cunning or sheep as stupid, merely serves to justify our treatment of these “dumb” animals.Jo BarlowTorquay, Devon
