articles.title: The Queensland ebike scheme keeping regional riders off the road: ‘If you live north of Rockhampton, bad luck’
articles.summary: New requirements ban electric bikes that have not been assessed at a registered retailer – of which there are only nine in the state
body: An ebike has saved Queensland mother Rhianna Steindl thousands of dollars in petrol and other vehicle running costs.

In the six years since she bought her large cargo bike, it has become a common sight in her regional town of Bundaberg. Steindl often uses it to commute to work, take the kids to school and more, giving up her car despite a lack of cycling infrastructure.
But a new law will probably prevent Steindl and other regional ebike users from being able to use their legal bikes.
Related: ‘Take them away, crush them’: Australia faces an ebike surge that some say poses a health emergency
Under new legislation passed by the Queensland state government earlier this year, e-vehicles are banned from use in public if they don’t meet a new standard capping their power at 250 watts.

Steindl says her ebike meets all the new requirements of the Electrically Power-Assisted Cycle (EPAC) assurance scheme but one: it doesn’t have the sticker that demonstrates it has been assessed at a bike retailer under the state’s new assurance scheme.
The state government quietly announced the scheme on 2 November. Just nine bike shops across the state have signed up.
Steindl’s nearest is 287km away in Rockhampton, the most northerly assurance location in the state. Owners have until just February to get their bike checked, at a capped cost of $70.

Active transport groups claim the scheme has become just the latest rushed feature of a crackdown they say has been done on the cheap and not properly thought through. They warn it risks ending the state’s e-vehicle revolution and forcing people back behind the wheel of a car.
Matt Burke, the CEO of Bikes Queensland, estimates that between 20,000 and 50,000 legal ebike across the state don’t have a sticker. He owns one of them.
A recent university of Queensland study backs this up. According to the study published last month, there are about 1m e-vehicles in the state, a fleet worth about $2.2bn.
Dr Richard Buning, the study’s author, estimates that there are 200,000 or more “legal” vehicles in the state that need a sticker.
Ebikes aren’t just common in the cities. A third of Queensland households own an e-mobility device, including about 28% of households in remote Queensland, the study found.
Burke said most big retailers have already declined to be part of the scheme because it isn’t worth their while and is labor intensive.
“This is a fiscal question. The government has chosen not to fund this appropriately, that’s what’s happened,” he said.
He said there will be no way for most owners in regional Queensland to get their vehicle accredited before an enforcement grace period runs out.
“If you live north of Rockhampton, bad luck,” he said. “There’s going to be no one within almost 700km of some of these cities, like Cairns and Townsville, where you can get your bike verified.
“So not the greatest outcome of a government service scheme.”
Some ebike owners argue that the Christmas holidays may complicate the scheme even further, given that, for many shops, it’s the busiest time of year.

Others are questioning why service centres operated by the Department of Transport and Main Roads (TMR) are not participating, given that they already do vehicle inspections for cars virtually everywhere in the state.
Peter Bourke, the general manager of Bicycle Industries Australia, said they are working with TMR to expand the scheme’s coverage across Queensland “very rapidly”, though it won’t be universal.

“We will be increasing the number of stores online. I’m hoping by the end of the month there will be 20 stores, with further stores in the new year that will be able to undertake verifications,” he said.

He said an assessment will take about half an hour to complete, so there should be no capacity problem. Bike shops were chosen as the delivery arm because they already had the skills, which TMR service centres do not, he said.

The TMR website says “alternative arrangements” will be available for those who live in a rural or remote area without reasonable access to an authorised verifier, “including the potential for a temporary, conditional permit”. It promises an update early next year. There are no further details available.
Like most of the world’s transport agencies, Queensland’s says it aims to encourage more people to give up their car and ride.

According to the Queensland Cycling Strategy 2017-2027, active transport “can reduce traffic congestion and have many health benefits for those who choose to cycle”, reduces the state’s carbon footprint and saves the state government money.

The department particularly commits to encouraging “active school travel” and to prioritise “people who need more support to start riding such as children, women and older people”, because they are the least likely to already cycle.
But Buning said the legislation risks undermining progress towards those goals.

He said ebike technology had had a “transformative” effect in Europe and Asia, proving to be a remarkably effective tool for shifting people out of a car, substantially increasing cycling rates – disproportionately among more vulnerable users – because ebikes don’t require as much physical fitness.
“The real benefit of e-mobility devices is it’s made active transport that much more attractive to just so much wider a segment of the population,” he said.
Related: Queensland has passed tough new laws on ebikes and e-scooters. What do they mean for riders, and will the world follow?
“There’s nothing in my time of researching this space for nearly two decades that’s encouraged people to want to use active transport as much.”

Queensland’s legislation targets exactly the groups the department wants to encourage to cycle, banning children under 16 and many old people from riding an e-vehicle at all. The first draft of the legislation would have also banned much of the state’s disabled community, but was amended to provide a medical exemption.

According to the law’s explanatory note, it was designed to force e-vehicle riders away from almost all of Brisbane’s safe cycling network into general traffic – which Buning said would also discourage female riders, who are known to be less risk averse.

The government-dominated Queensland parliamentary committee, which recommended the legislation, heard that there is no evidence of any public safety risk associated with legal ebikes. It identified just a single fatal accident involving a legal ebike during its year-long inquiry, an elderly woman killed by a car.
Buning’s research shows that, for a quarter of the state’s e-mobility users, a private car is their only alternative, particularly in regional areas.
“If you live in one of those areas, you have no access to public transport. You have no other access way of getting around.”
Burke said the scheme had been rushed and not properly thought through. Queensland is falling behind the rest of the world, he said.
“Queensland is slow on the adoption of e-mobility and of cycling more generally,” he said.
“New York has just tripled in recent years, Paris has multiplied it by about seven times. London has had really steep increases.
“We’re not in a good space in Queensland. We will be even more behind where everyone else in the world is headed.”
A spokesperson for Transport and Main Roads said the scheme is “already helping Queenslanders retain and use eligible devices safely and legally”.
“Authorised verification locations are now operating across the state and more locations are expected to come online in the coming weeks,” they said.
Steindl says she has given up riding the ebike as a result of the legislation and instead drives her four-wheel drive everywhere. Diesel is now among her highest household bills.
“You know what? It’s just easier to get in the car,” she said.

articles.title: World’s top court to rule if Myanmar committed genocide against Rohingya
articles.summary: International court of justice has never before found a state guilty of genocide, and ruling will have implications for case against Israel
body: The world’s top court will deliver a judgment this week on whether Myanmar committed genocide against its Rohingya minority, in a landmark case that will set a critical 21st-century benchmark for the gravest of all international crimes.
The closely watched judgment could become one of the most significant moments in international law since the end of the second world war.

The international court of justice (ICJ) has never found a state responsible for genocide, a crime defined after the Nazi-led Holocaust. The ruling will have implications for a separate high-profile genocide case against Israel.
Nearly a decade after a military campaign forced hundreds of thousands of Muslim Rohingya to flee across the border, the ICJ in The Hague will deliver its judgment on Thursday morning.
“The ICJ ruling will be historic for Rohingya survivors and their families around the world,” said Yanghee Lee, a former UN rights investigator to Myanmar.

“The international community failed to prevent Myanmar military atrocities against the Rohingya nine years ago. It must seize this opportunity to finally secure justice for the Rohingya and begin to reckon with these failings.”
ICJ judges have spent seven years weighing accusations by the Gambia, a Muslim-majority state, that Myanmar’s repression of the Rohingya breached the 1948 UN genocide convention.
A key issue in previous cases has been how to prove “intent” in a crime defined as acts committed with the “intent to destroy, in whole or in part” a national, ethnical, racial or religious group.

Antonia Mulvey, the founder of Legal Action Worldwide (Law), a group that represents hundreds of Rohingya survivors, said she was “cautiously optimistic” the court would hold Myanmar fully accountable.
Government actions showed “patterns of conduct” that proved clear attempts to destroy the group, she said.

“The attacks on the villages took place the same way,” she said. “They would attack the civilians, burn the villages, separate men and women, conduct sexual violence … and then as they fled, they would continue to kill them.”
Related: Massacre at Tula Toli: Rohingya recall horror of Myanmar army attack

Two other ICJ cases dealing with atrocities in the Balkans fell short of finding states directly responsible for genocide, although Serbia was found legally responsible for failing to prevent the genocide at Srebrenica.

Mulvey said a key part of the upcoming judgment will be how it handles the issue of rape and sexual violence as an act of genocide. Her team has collected accounts of soldiers mutilating women’s genitals and biting their faces. “That’s to mark people, to brand them … it is also to stop reproduction,” she said.
“Yes, we would say sexual violence is a critical part to show their intent to destroy the group,” she added.

“You don’t need to gang-rape people. You don’t need to kill their children in front of them. You don’t need to mutilate them. You don’t need to do it in public. What is the purpose of that? The purpose is to destroy the group.”

In January, the ICJ held closed-door sessions to hear directly from Rohingya survivors who travelled from camps in Bangladesh. One witness said her child was taken from her arms, stabbed and thrown into a fire, according to Law, while another described seeing piles of bodies in a mass grave.
During hearings, Gambian justice minister Dawda Jallow told the court the case was not “about esoteric issues of international law”.
“It is about real people, real stories and a real group of human beings,” said Jallow. “The Rohingya of Myanmar. They have been targeted for destruction.”
Related: ‘They showed no mercy’: mapping the Rohingya villages being erased by rebel forces
Myanmar, which has denied carrying out a genocide, claims its actions targeted a military uprising from insurgents.

For decades, Rohingya people have been stripped of their citizenship and targeted by increasing discrimination, amid a backdrop of communal violence with Buddhists in the country’s western Rakhine state.
The crisis reached a climax after a Rohingya militant group conducted guerrilla-style attacks in the summer of 2017. The Myanmar army responded with massive “clearance operations”.

Refugees who fled into Bangladesh in 2017 told the Guardian of a massacre in the village of Tula Toli, where survivors described systematic shooting of civilians, including the drowning of children in a river.
This testimony from Tula Toli – which satellite footage later showed had been razed – added to dozens of witness accounts collected over the years to build a case for genocide.

A ruling that Myanmar committed genocide would add international pressure on its leader Min Aung Hlaing, who headed the military during the 2016-2017 attacks and later overthrew the elected government of Aung San Suu Kyi in a 2021 coup, triggering a civil war that has left tens of thousands dead.

The former general is separately b​eing investigated by the international criminal court (ICC), which prosecutes individuals and not states like the ICJ, on allegations of crimes against humanity. He was installed as civilian president in April after elections that were widely condemned as a sham, and has made efforts to rebuild diplomatic ties.

For many onlookers, the ICJ decision will hold relevance far beyond Myanmar, as it will provide the strongest hint of how judges might assess the seminal genocide case brought by South Africa against Israel over its campaign in Gaza.
The cases have much in common, with an ethnic group targeted by a powerful military, although Israel has far stronger diplomatic backing from the US.

The judgment comes as Washington has been on the offensive against international human rights bodies, including sanctioning the ICC. Washington technically already considers the Rohingya crisis to be a genocide, based on a decision by the Biden administration.

However, Trump’s UN ambassador, Mike Waltz, warned that the ICJ “must not be allowed” to establish a standard for genocide that could be used against “allied soldiers”, a statement that will be relevant for Israeli troops.

Supporters of the Myanmar case say the judgment should compel states to block arms transfers and jet fuel supplies. While the court does not have the means to enforce its decisions, they have been respected in the past, and the UN security council could give it strength, although divisions, especially between the US and China, make this unlikely.
More than 1 million Rohingya remain in Bangladesh, in the world’s largest refugee settlement. Fewer than 600,000 are estimated to remain in Myanmar.
A displaced Rohingya living inside Myanmar told the Guardian he hoped the judgment would “help end decades of persecution and discrimination”.
“We are not asking for sympathy alone,” he said. “We are asking for justice, recognition, equal rights and a future in which our children can live safely and with dignity in their own homeland.”

articles.title: ‘We need to get back to class’: some teachers lose patience as France enters its eighth week of student protests
articles.summary: Educators voice concerns as thousands of children facing exams miss up to 150 hours of class
body: For several weeks, Alex, 16, has woken at 4am and walked 90 minutes in the dark from his northern Paris suburb so he can help gather wheelie bins to blockade his high school in Vincennes.

In a tote bag, he brings some masks and some swimming goggles in case of police teargas. His parents, who work in the arts and vote left, support the French school student protesters who since September have blocked schools demanding repairs to dilapidated school buildings, more replacement teachers, a solution to overcrowded classes and more equality in the university application system.

“But this week, my mum woke up early and said to me: ‘Do you really think you need to blockade again today?’’ said Alex. “She supports me but is starting to think I’m doing too much. But how else can we make ourselves heard? We can’t stop now. It’s the only way the government will listen.”
His 17-year-old friend, also on the school barricade with dozens of pupils this week, said: “Any progress that has been won in France has been achieved through people demonstrating on the street.”
Related: ‘A global political awakening’: how gen Z protests are sweeping the world

France is entering the eighth week of an unprecedented schools crisis. The biggest youth protest movement in decades has over the past two months seen hundreds of high schools barricaded with wheelie bins or shut amid security fears.

The government is now facing criticism of its handling of the crisis. It first responded with a security crackdown, mobilising riot police outside schools across France amid clashes that led to injuries from police weaponry, including children who lost a hand or an eye.
Then over the past two weeks, the government attempted to argue that its offer to decrease some class sizes and review the university application platform meant the movement was coming to an end.

But in recent days, the government has been accused by teachers’ unions of letting the protests fester into an increasingly dangerous mood of violence. Fireworks have been fired outside schools and inside classrooms in different parts of France.

A local councillor outside Paris was hit in the chest by a bottle of gasoline as she was trying to mediate outside a school. One education trade unionist said a school principal had bought a bulletproof vest for protection.
The government and teachers’ unions have said that individuals committing violence outside or inside schools were not the same people as students who were peacefully protesting for education rights.

But high school principals held their own demonstrations on Friday, saying they were struggling to cope with the confusion and chaos. At least 50 principals have made requests to quit their posts. More than 360 schoolchildren and 245 staff have been injured since the protests started.

So many weeks of classes have now been missed that one teacher, who demonstrated outside a central Paris police station this week after one of her pupils was arrested, said: “There is absolute uncertainty over how we can return to proper teaching. This is becoming an intractable situation with no end in sight.”

Thousands of French children in key baccalauréat (the French A-levels) exam years – even children who are not protesting directly – have now missed up to 150 hours of teaching at schools that have been barricaded daily or closed regularly for security reasons since the end of September. This is particularly acute in the Paris area, and in other cities such as Toulouse.

Online lessons have rarely fully replaced missed classes. Many teenagers are at home in their fourth or fifth week of no school. Some parents are beginning to wake early to stand outside schools themselves to try to individually stop wheelie bin barricades – sometimes leading to more clashes.
Police are increasingly stationed outside schools, sometimes hitting students’ hands with truncheons to make them loosen their grip on bins, as happened in central Paris this week.

“The French administration is trying to impose a kind of smokescreen of wishful thinking, that everything is alright, stiff-upper-lip, no problem, but everyone needs to face up to what is happening,” said Julien Roy, 52, who teaches history and geography at Lycée Balzac in the central city of Tours and represents the SNALC education union in Indre-et-Loire. “There is a crisis of trust. We need a de-escalation of violence and a path back to education.”

Roy’s school has been at the centre of the protests since the end of September when, on the pavement outside, a 16-year-old school student from a different school, lost the use of his eye after he was allegedly struck by a police rubber bullet.

“There is still constant tension,” said Roy. He added that in recent weeks firework mortars had been set off, sometimes aimed at staff, and fires had been started in bins and materials for molotov cocktails were found in a building opposite the school.

Police were regularly present. Staff felt individuals not connected to the school were involved in the violence. He said stress was taking a toll on staff: 10 colleagues were on sick leave, including his principal and deputy principal.

“We need to get back to class to teach our pupils again, some of whom are booing us,” Roy said. “We’ll have to sit down and talk about this, honestly and calmly, to get it out of everyone’s system so we can restore trust.”

He said: “There are children who are suffering, and many of them we’re not seeing because they are stuck at home. Some pupils approach school, see the police, panic and go away, because they can’t bear this atmosphere with police outside school. There are fragile teenagers with difficulties at school who can’t come in, and those children are shattered by this.”

He said: “What is lethal is that we’re leading children to conclude that it’s only through violence that they can be heard, that violence is legitimate and nothing can be gained through negotiation … this is going to leave an impact on society, creating future adults who are going to feel bitter and broken.”

At a high school in the Créteil area, an English teacher said: “I feel proud of my students’ peaceful protests. The children demonstrating are asking for the same thing teachers have wanted for years: more resources, more dignity in teaching environments. Teachers’ strikes haven’t been listened to, whereas students see they are having an impact.

“But with a presidential election next spring, and the start of electoral season, it’s difficult to imagine that this is going to stop. I do worry about students’ exams. One former colleague said to me that this school year could be a write-off.”
Students’ names have been changed

articles.title: World leaders head to Asia for back-to-back diplomatic summits
articles.summary: Tussle for influence as trade, tech and regional security to take centre stage in China, Philippines and Cambodia meetings
body: World leaders will fly in to Asia for back-to-back high-level summits this week against the backdrop of the tussle for influence between the superpowers China and the US.

Beijing will have the home advantage when it welcomes Donald Trump to its southern technology hub of Shenzhen for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) leaders’ meeting. It starts two weeks after the US leader lost midterm elections.

The summit also comes after an awkward-at-best revelation that the head of Nvidia, the US chipmaker that for a long time was the world’s most valuable company, was having an affair with a woman US intelligence suspects was a Chinese spy.

Apec represents more than 60% of global GDP and has primarily promoted free trade and multilateralism. This year’s meeting could be defined, however, by the confirmed trilateral meeting between Trump, the Chinese president, Xi Jinping, and Vladimir Putin of Russia.

The three-way meeting has been likened to a modern-day Yalta, when in 1945 then US president, Franklin D Roosevelt, Britain’s Winston Churchill and the Soviet leader Joseph Stalin met in Crimea to carve up Europe after the second world war. However, analysts say a “Yalta 2.0” that issues edicts on Ukraine and Taiwan without their involvement is unlikely.

Xiaoyu Pu, an associate professor at the University of Nevada’s department of political science, said a three-way meeting “might be more symbolic than substantive, although symbolism itself matters in great-power diplomacy.

“Trump appears interested in nuclear arms control and denuclearisation. Xi’s priority is likely to maintain a stable relationship with Washington while preserving China’s strategic partnership with Russia. Putin, meanwhile, wants to maintain his bargaining leverage over Ukraine.”

Apec begins on Wednesday and follows a flurry of other diplomatic gatherings, chief among them the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean) meeting in the Philippines, starting on Sunday, which Trump will attend.

While he is in Manila, US officials will hold a sidelines meeting of the so-called Quad – Australia, India, Japan and the US. In addition, a Francophone summit, which includes the Canadian prime minister, Mark Carney, and the French president, Emmanuel Macron, is happening concurrently in Cambodia.

Critical global issues at all these summits will include AI supply chains and governance, tariff reductions and the green energy transition. Trump’s focus has been on denuclearisation. A key regional focus will be on the South China Sea, where Beijing has built massive military outposts in disputed waters, as well as the gigantic Indonesian forest fire haze blanketing the region.

The humanitarian and security crisis in Myanmar has become a perennial issue, as is status of Taiwan, which China does not recognise. The self-ruled island is sending the founder of the tech hardware company Acer as its envoy to Apec.

For well over a decade, Washington’s engagement in the region has been coloured by concern over the rise of China, with the then president Barack Obama telling Australia’s parliament in 2011 that the US was “a Pacific power, and we are here to stay” – a policy known as the “pivot to Asia”.
The strategy of intense diplomacy and trade deals was adopted by Joe Biden, who hoped to gather allies on the continent who wanted to balance their relationships with both superpowers.

Some analysts see Trump’s transactional style in Asia as a continuation of the pivot policy. Still, the president’s volatility and unpredictability have spooked smaller nations, who regard China as a more predictable partner.

Jayant Menon, an economist at Singapore’s Iseas-Yusof Ishak Institute, said that countries in south-east Asia had been “laying the groundwork for a future with reduced dependence on the United States” by seeking deals elsewhere, including with each other and the EU.

“Amid persistent uncertainty and an administration determined to levy tariffs by any legal means, south-east Asia’s ability to ride out another round of tariffs depends on deeper regional integration and diversification beyond the US market,” he wrote this month in the East Asia Forum.

Beijing’s more predictable policies do not necessarily make it any more palatable for its regional neighbours, however, and the Chinese premier, Li Qiang, could have tough talks when he goes to Manila for the Asean summit, especially on the South China Sea.
China’s top diplomat, Wang Yi, recently urged Manila to rein in Filipino politicians who he said had repeatedly “smeared” Beijing, after public outcries in the country over the disputed waters.

Brunei, China, Malaysia, the Philippines, Taiwan and Vietnam have been locked in decades-long territorial standoffs in the busy waterway, which could sit on deposits of oil and gas. Washington has sent military ships on “freedom of navigation operations”, despite Chinese outcries, although US-linked crises in Iran, Ukraine, Venezuela, and Palestine and Israel have sucked up Washington’s focus under Trump’s second term.

A decades-long attempt to sign a South China Sea pact is not expected to happen at this year’s Asean summit, as previously hoped. Despite monthly meetings, negotiations will have to continue next year, when Asean’s leadership rotates to Singapore.

Diplomats at the Asean summit will also be focusing on Myanmar, which is seeking reintegration. Each country in the group is assessing how to deal with their isolated neighbour. The timing of summits this week coincides with a judgment in the international court of justice on Thursday that could find Myanmar responsible for genocide. The coup leader, Min Aung Hlaing, remains barred from Asean but is allowed to send a representative.
Asia’s week of diplomacy will be followed next month by the G20 summit in Miami, Florida, which Xi is expected to attend if US and Chinese relations continue to hold steady.
Additional research by Yu-chen Li

articles.title: Ukraine war briefing: US proposes Kyiv cede land to Russia for Nato membership, Zelenskyy says
articles.summary: Ukrainian president says Kyiv not ready to concede Donbas but would put idea to a referendum in exchange for security guarantees and funding. What we know on day 1,726
body: Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said the US has asked for the first time if Ukraine would withdraw from parts of the eastern Donbas region that Russia does not control in exchange for Ukraine becoming a Nato member. But the Ukrainian president said his country would not surrender territory. “The Americans raised a question: ‘What if Ukraine joins Nato? Would Ukraine withdraw from Donbas?’,” he said in remarks to reporters released by his office on Saturday. “That is why ⁠I believe Nato is back on the agenda.” But he said the suggestion, which would form part of a new postwar security framework for Europe, could allow Russia to weaken Nato and reshape borders. “This is dangerous because, in my view, it is precisely things like this that lead to wars or escalations,” Zelenskyy said.

Zelenskyy reiterated his position that Kyiv was not ready to concede territory but said that if it received a comprehensive package including security guarantees, the right to a strong and well-funded ​Ukrainian army and funds to rebuild, he would put the question to a ‌national referendum. Echoing comments ‌made by European leaders at a summit in Dublin on Friday, Zelenskyy dismissed Russia’s call for a broad agreement on European security architecture to be reached before the specifics are ‌agreed on how to end the war in Ukraine. “We cannot turn everything upside down and start by talking about changing the security framework in the world or across the continent overall, and only then talk about ending this war. This war must be ended first,” he said.

The Ukrainian president has also rejected the possibility of Ukraine committing to neutrality, something that could only happen if the country’s constitution was changed. “If Putin expects Ukraine’s neutrality to be enshrined, that’s not going to happen,” he said. “We’re not in Nato right now anyway.”

US President ⁠Donald Trump’s ⁠envoy and ​son-in-law Jared ⁠Kushner said on ⁠Saturday ​the US ‌was ‌focused on ‌facilitating direct engagement between Russia and ‌European nations on ​the Ukraine war, ⁠after trilateral meetings ​involving Washington, ​Moscow ​and ​Kyiv ‌this ​week. However, Washington and Nato have not yet commented on the suggestion of a swap of the Donbas for Ukraine Nato membership. Negotiations did, however, lead to agreements that European countries would join future talks on ending the war.

Zelenskyy has accused SpaceX of not telling the truth over restrictions to Ukraine’s Starshield satellite system, saying the decision to impose speed limits appears to be “political” rather than “technical”. Speaking on Friday, Ukraine’s president said the restrictions affecting Ukrainian drones, in place for five days, meant they could no longer intercept incoming jet-powered Russian Shahed drones. Ukraine suspects the slowdown is a deliberate US tactic, designed to put pressure on Zelenskyy to make concessions to Putin.

French President Emmanuel Macron said Saturday that countries seeking to limit aid to Ukraine want to impose an “unjust peace” and warned that it was a recipe for another war. “Those who want to ration aid to Ukraine wish underneath it all to force an unjust peace on it” and, by extension, all of Europe, Macron said on social media. “That is a recipe for another war. That cannot be France’s position.”

Russian forces ⁠struck a cargo vessel in ⁠the ⁠Ukrainian ​port of Chornomorsk, RIA ⁠news agency cited the Russian ⁠defence ministry ​as ‌saying on ‌Saturday. The ministry ‌said the ship was being used to supply the Ukrainian ‌military. Meanwhile, Ukrainian strikes on the Samara oil pipeline station near the village of Prosvet in Russia’s Samara region on Friday set several oil storage tanks on fire, Ukraine’s General Staff said. The facility is a key part of the network exporting Russian oil to global markets, the General Staff said. Separately, 22 people were injured in a Russian attack on the south-east Ukrainian city of Zaporizhzhia on Friday, Ukraine’s Emergency Service said.

articles.title: US officials say flight stoppage stemmed from ‘routine maintenance’ as travel chaos continues
articles.summary: Thousands of flights still canceled as officials blamed ageing air control system for nationwide grounding
body: The Trump administration says Friday’s four-hour nationwide Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) ground stop that delayed or canceled thousands of flight stemmed from routine maintenance.

At a news briefing on Saturday, the US transportation secretary, Sean Duffy, said that the issues began when a contractor was performing “routine maintenance” at a remote FAA facility to “switch telecommunications lines” from copper wire to fiber optic cable.
“What we’re working to determine is whether we had incompetence,” Duffy said, “or did they install a faulty router.”
He added: “Once we were able to isolate the work that was being done at this remote location, all of our systems came back online,” and the ground stop was lifted.
However, travel chaos continued across the US on Saturday.
At the briefing, the FAA’s head, Bryan Bedford, apologized to passengers and said he believed that the worst of the disruption “is behind us”.

“We will still have delays and cancellations today, but that will set us up for a full recovery tomorrow,” Bedford said. “Based on everything that we’re hearing from our airline partners, they believe that they’ll be able to have full schedule integrity by the close of business on Sunday.”

“I want to reiterate: we see zero evidence of anything nefarious, and zero evidence of anything AI-related,” he continued. “So we want to be clear that we have a equipment issue, and we’re working through what this defective piece of equipment was.”

Later on Saturday, L3Harris, the federal contractor that Duffy said had been updating air traffic control equipment before the ground stop, released a statement saying that it took the ground stop and its negative effects “on travelers, airlines and air traffic operations seriously”.
The contractor said that it had completed more than 70% of the planned airspace communications conversion from legacy copper wires to a fiber optic system.
“We are supporting the FAA in its investigation to understand the conditions that led to the [Friday] ground stop of our nation’s air travel,” the contractor said.
On Saturday,airlines worked to recover from Friday’s four-hour nationwide Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) ground stop that delayed or canceled thousands of flights.

By of 11am ET on Saturday morning, more than 4,000 flights within, into or out of the US had already been canceled, according to FlightAware, adding to the more than 8,000 cancellations recorded on Friday.

The disruption, which marked the longest nationwide ground stop in 25 years, left passengers stranded at airports across the country and facing uncertainty about when they could reach their destinations.
Related: What to know about the rare nationwide ground stop issued by the FAA

Duffy on Friday had blamed the ground stop on an ageing air control system, saying that the communications equipment became “overloaded with data” and was starting to cause inconsistency in the data”.
“Because of that, we shut the system down,” Duffy said.
Duffy on Saturday again mentioned the US having a “decades-old air traffic control system”. “It’s not just old equipment – we have an incredibly old telecommunications system,” he said.
“The work happening was due to the age of the copper wire that we were replacing,” Duffy said on Saturday. “What we’re working to determine was whether … it [was] user error or installer error.”
Duffy echoed Bedford in saying “we don’t believe” the disruption resulted from a cyber-attack or some hostile foreign nation.
“This was an FAA system that didn’t meet the moment,” he said. “Our contractor didn’t meet the moment or the equipment didn’t meet the moment and causes the outages.”
Duffy also warned that it would “take us time” to “resume normal operations”.

Among those affected by the fallout from the ground stop on Friday were sports teams traveling for games over the weekend. In college football, the Southeastern Conference announced that Mississippi’s game against Oklahoma had been rescheduled to Sunday – a day usually reserved for the National Football League (NFL).

Meanwhile, a men’s college basketball game between the University of North Carolina Greensboro and Cornell University, scheduled for Saturday, was postponed. NBA and NHL travel was also disrupted for the weekend.
On Saturday morning, there were reported flight disruptions at airports in major cities including Boston, Washington DC, New York and Miami.

American Airlines said in a statement on Saturday that “while we are taking every step to limit the impact on our customers and team members, the lingering effects of this major disruption to the national airspace system will continue today, including additional delays and cancellations”.

Delta Air Lines also warned passengers traveling on Saturday that they “should expect delays and additional schedule adjustments as we work to reposition flight crews and aircraft” after the FAA-ordered ground stop.

The UK’s Civil Aviation Authority (CAA) also issued a statement on Saturday morning warning that “while US flights have resumed, there may be some follow-on disruption as airlines work to re-book affected passengers and get all services back to normal”.

Friday marked the third nationwide ground stop issued by the FAA this century. The first occurred after the 11 September 2001 terrorist attacks. And the second took place in January 2023, during the Biden administration, after a pilot notification system went down.

During Friday’s briefing, Trump administration officials urged Congress – which until January is controlled by the White House’s Republican allies – to “fully fund a full build of a brand new air traffic control system”.

Meanwhile, on Saturday, New York’s governor, Kathy Hochul, a Democrat, called on Duffy to resign. She also called on Congress to “launch a full investigation to determine what went wrong and ensure it never happens again”.
